title: Boosted trees characterize distressing hot flashes after breast cancer treatment
summary: LightGBM analysis of cross-sectional surveys from 360 early-breast-cancer patients associated reported hot-flash frequency and age with symptom-related distress. Nested internal validation gave AUC 0.731, and partial-dependence analysis suggested greater distress around seventeen or more hot flashes per week. This characterizes concurrent symptoms, not future toxicity or treatment efficacy. Recall bias, inconsistent survey-scale origins and predictors reflecting responses to existing symptoms limit interpretation.
ai_technology: LightGBM gradient-boosted decision trees; conditional partial dependence
organization: University of Ottawa; Ottawa Hospital Research Institute; Western University

source_review.scope: Primary relevant outcome definition, predictor construction, LightGBM and nested-validation Methods, results and limitations. Supplementary Appendix C was not inspected. Exact primary identity/date and fresh primary PubMed correction/retraction relationships checked.

evidence.tested: Survey-derived classification of current high versus low Hot Flush Night Sweats problem scores, with nested ten-fold outer/five-fold inner validation, Bayesian tuning and permutation-and-retraining importance.
evidence.unknown: Prospective symptom forecasts, independent validation and benefits of symptom screening or medication remain unestablished. Drug use and cancer-treatment changes may follow rather than precede severe symptoms; the symptom threshold is exploratory.
evidence.ai_role: Boosted trees learn nonlinear relationships among survey measurements and current reported symptom burden, with conditional partial dependence characterizing frequency/age associations.
